The iron-triangle trade-off among access, cost, and quality, attributed to William Kissick (1994)
The policymaking process: problem, agenda, legislation, rulemaking, implementation, evaluation
Roles of Congress, federal agencies (notice-and-comment rulemaking), states, and courts
Major policy levers: coverage expansion, payment/delivery reform, regulation, public health
Four landmark US laws as dated facts: SSA amendments 1965 (Medicare/Medicaid), EMTALA 1986, HIPAA 1996, ACA 2010
Contested policy questions (role of government; cost control vs access) presented as contested and attributed

claims.claim: Health policy is the set of goals, decisions, laws, and rules governments and other authoritative actors use to influence a population's health and the system that serves it; its three recurring goals are access, cost, and quality.

The 'iron triangle' of health care — the tension among access, cost containment, and quality, where improving one usually compromises another — was introduced by William Kissick in his 1994 book Medicine's Dilemmas (Yale University Press).

A federal bill is introduced by a member of Congress, studied in committee, must pass both the House and the Senate, and is then signed or vetoed by the President; statutes commonly delegate operational detail to executive agencies.

Under the Administrative Procedure Act (5 U.S.C. 553), agencies issue binding regulations through notice-and-comment rulemaking: publishing a proposed rule in the Federal Register, taking public comment, and issuing a final rule.
The Social Security Amendments of 1965 (Pub. L. 89-97, approved July 30, 1965) added Titles XVIII and XIX to the Social Security Act, creating Medicare and Medicaid.

EMTALA, enacted in 1986 and codified at 42 U.S.C. 1395dd, requires Medicare-participating hospitals with emergency departments to provide a medical screening examination and to stabilize or appropriately transfer anyone with an emergency medical condition, regardless of insurance status or ability to pay.
HIPAA was enacted in 1996 (Pub. L. 104-191); it addressed insurance portability and administrative simplification and is the basis of later health-information privacy and security standards.

The Patient Protection and Affordable Care Act (Pub. L. 111-148) was signed March 23, 2010; it created subsidized insurance marketplaces, set new insurer rules, and offered states funding to expand Medicaid.

In NFIB v. Sebelius (2012) the Supreme Court held that the federal government could not withdraw a state's existing Medicaid funds for declining the ACA expansion, effectively making the expansion optional for states.
U.S. national health expenditures reached $5.3 trillion, or 18.0 percent of GDP ($15,474 per person), in 2024.
Public opinion on the ACA is divided and partisan; around the law's sixteenth anniversary, KFF polling found it viewed favorably by most Democrats and unfavorably by most Republicans.

How large a role government should play in financing and regulating care, and whether to prioritize cost control or coverage when they conflict, are genuinely contested value questions rather than settled technical facts.

conflictingEvidence.issue: How large a role government should play in financing and regulating health care
positions: Some hold that broader public financing (and stronger regulation of insurers and prices) is the surest route to universal access and cost control
Others hold that market competition and consumer choice deliver better quality and restrain spending more effectively than government provision
conflictingEvidence.resolution: Presented as a genuinely contested value question; positions are attributed to broad schools of thought and none is endorsed. KFF polling is cited only to establish that opinion is divided and partisan, not to favor a side.

conflictingEvidence.issue: Whether the iron-triangle trade-offs are truly rigid
positions: Kissick's original framing treats access, cost, and quality as a roughly zero-sum, 'iron' trade-off
Later commentators argue the trade-offs can sometimes be eased by eliminating waste or improving efficiency
conflictingEvidence.resolution: The lesson presents the iron triangle as an attributed conceptual model, notes the critique, and does not assert it as a law of nature.

unsupportedExistingClaims: The generated draft contained only generic boilerplate (e.g., 'Health Policy is a foundational concept... a simple way to apply it') with no substantive, verifiable claims; nothing in it was usable as evidence.
correctionsNeeded: Replaced the boilerplate definition with a sourced definition tied to the goals of access, cost, and quality.
Added the attributed iron-triangle concept (Kissick, 1994) in place of vague 'context/evidence/application' vocabulary.
Added the actual policymaking process and the four dated landmark laws, none of which appeared in the draft.
Added explicit treatment of contested questions as contested, with attribution.
rightsIssues: Penn LDI and KFF pages are secondary explainers used REFERENCE_ONLY; no wording was reproduced. Kissick's book is referenced by title and attribution only, not quoted.
Federal statutes, U.S. Code sections, the Supreme Court opinion, and government agency pages are U.S. government works (public domain or freely usable); all prose is original synthesis.

sourceRecords.title: William Kissick and the Iron Triangle of Health Economics
sourceRecords.provider: Leonard Davis Institute of Health Economics, University of Pennsylvania
sourceRecords.notes: Read via WebFetch. Supports the attribution of the iron triangle to William Kissick, MD, PhD, MPH; the 1994 book 'Medicine's Dilemmas: Infinite Needs Versus Finite Resources' (Yale University Press); the three corners (access, quality, cost containment); and the trade-off that any one corner can be improved only by compromising one or both of the others. Used as a REFERENCE_ONLY secondary explainer from the institute Kissick helped shape; no wording reproduced.

sourceRecords.title: The Legislative Process (The House Explained)
sourceRecords.notes: Read via curl with a browser user-agent (congress.gov and the direct page are behind an interstitial to the plain fetcher). Supports the description of how a bill becomes law: a representative sponsors a bill, it is assigned to committee for study, if released it is placed on a calendar to be debated, amended, and voted on, must pass both the House (simple majority, 218 of 435) and the Senate, and then goes to the President. Used for the legislative-steps portion of the policymaking process.

sourceRecords.title: 5 U.S.C. 553 - Rule making (United States Code, 2023 Edition)
sourceRecords.provider: Office of the Law Revision Counsel / U.S. Government Publishing Office (govinfo)
sourceRecords.license: U.S. Code; edict of government, not subject to copyright
sourceRecords.notes: Reused from the source registry (id and URL unchanged). Supports notice-and-comment rulemaking: subsection (b) requires general notice of proposed rule making published in the Federal Register; subsection (c) requires an opportunity to submit written data, views, or arguments and a concise general statement of basis and purpose; subsection (d) requires publication at least 30 days before a substantive rule's effective date. Used for how agencies turn statutes into binding rules.

sourceRecords.title: Emergency Medical Treatment & Labor Act (EMTALA)
sourceRecords.notes: cms.gov returned a JavaScript/interstitial body to WebFetch; the page shell and EMTALA description were read via curl with a browser user-agent, and the substantive requirements were cross-checked against 42 U.S.C. 1395dd (uscode.house.gov) and the Congress.gov CRS product IF12355. Supports that EMTALA was enacted in 1986, that it applies to Medicare-participating hospitals with emergency departments, and that it requires a medical screening examination and stabilization or appropriate transfer regardless of ability to pay. Canonical CMS description page; no wording reproduced.

sourceRecords.title: 42 U.S.C. 1395dd - Examination and treatment for emergency medical conditions and women in labor
sourceRecords.provider: Office of the Law Revision Counsel, U.S. Code (uscode.house.gov)
sourceRecords.license: U.S. Code; edict of government, not subject to copyright
sourceRecords.notes: Read via WebFetch. Supports the statutory duties: an appropriate medical screening examination for any individual who comes to the emergency department; stabilizing treatment or an appropriate transfer for an emergency medical condition; restrictions on transferring unstabilized patients; and a prohibition on delaying screening to inquire about payment or insurance. Used as the codified primary text behind EMTALA.

sourceRecords.title: After 16 Years, Partisans Still View the Affordable Care Act Very Differently
sourceRecords.notes: Read via WebSearch summary of KFF tracking-poll results around the ACA's sixteenth anniversary: the law viewed favorably overall (about 61%) but with a wide partisan split (roughly 90% of Democrats favorable versus about 32% of Republicans). Used only to support the claim that public opinion on health policy is divided and partisan, illustrating that value questions are contested; figures attributed to KFF and dated.
